newsitem.title: USA: Dollar mixed as market weighs Dow slide, higher rates.
newsitem.headline: Dollar mixed as market weighs Dow slide, higher rates.

text.p: The dollar edged higher against the German mark and the Japanese yen on Friday, but support from expectations of higher interest rates was offset by a sharp sell-off in stocks.
The dollar slipped, however, against the Swiss franc.

Reports on wholesale prices and retail sales pointed to a still-strong U.S. economy and raised fears that the Federal Reserve would raise interest rates again, prompting the sharp selloff in stocks and bonds.
While higher interest rates generally support a stronger dollar, the sell-off in stocks led to concern that investors might unload dollar-denominated assets and sell dollars.
The Dow Jones industrial average dropped 148.36 points Friday to 6,391.69.
John Nelson, foreign exchange trading manager at ABN-AMRO Bank in Chicago, said he felt that the possibility of higher interest rates offset the pressure coming from the weaker stocks.
"High U.S. interest rates are clearly benefiting the dollar more than sales of U.S.-dollar-denominated assets (are hurting it)," Nelson said.

"You have to own dollars for the interest rate differential," added Russell LaScala head of spot foreign exchange trading at Citibank. "The economy is steaming ahead at 3 to 4 percent and inflation looks like it is going to be a problem in the future."
The dollar closed at 1.7205 marks compared with 1.7190 marks on Thursday and at 126.12 yen compared with 125.85 yen. It fell to 1.4610 Swiss francs from 1.4685 Swiss.

The economic reports fuelling the interest rate fears included a report showing core wholesale prices, excluding volatile food and energy costs, rose 0.4 percent in March after falling the month before.
In a revision to previous data, the government said retail sales rose 1.5 percent in February, much stronger than first reported, although sales were up a more tame 0.2 percent in March.

The dollar rose briefly in early trade Friday. It gained against the yen after Kabun Muto, a member of the Japanese cabinet, said he thought it unlikely that the dollar strength could be checked by "artificial" attempts to prop up the yen, an apparent reference to warnings this week that the Japanese Ministry of Finance could intervene to strengthen the yen.

That rally was cut short when the ministry distanced itself from Muto's remarks. The ministry said the official view remains that the yen's falls are overdone and the goverment remains concerned about it.

"Muto's commment was quickly put in perspective ... it was quickly said he was not representing the Japanese government and the (Ministry of Finance) was a little bit clearer in their position referring to the word 'excessive' again," said Stephen Flanagan, a vice president at Credit Agricole in New York.
Elsewhere, the dollar rose to Canadian $1.3983 from C$1.3937. The Bank of Canada tried to support its sagging currency by buying Canadian dollars in the market.
The British pound rose to $1.6275 from $1.6230.
